strengths: The reduction from Multicolored Clique to two-layer ReLU positivity is conceptually clean and appears to provide a meaningful W[1]-hardness result with input dimension linear in the clique parameter.
The homogenization argument plausibly transfers the positivity result to bias-free networks, surjectivity, and zonotope non-containment, yielding relevant ETH-based lower bounds.

The paper is well organized, clearly motivates the parameterized-complexity questions, and provides extensive appendices and useful connections among neural-network verification, zonotopes, and norm maximization.
weaknesses: The proof of Theorem 6.2 relies on the false assertion that every positively homogeneous CPWL function satisfies L_p(f)=max_{||x||_p<=1}|f(x)|. For example, f(x1,x2)=ReLU(x1)-ReLU(x2) has L_2(f)=sqrt(2), while the stated maximum is 1. Lipschitz constants depend on all local gradients, not only values along rays from the origin.

This error directly invalidates the proposed Lipschitz reduction: scaling the homogenizing y-coefficients shrinks the heights and locations of the spike functions but leaves their slopes with respect to x essentially unchanged. Consequently, the claimed bound L_p(h)<=max_x h(x,1), which is central to the completeness/soundness gap, can fail dramatically. Thus a major advertised contribution—W[1]-hardness of exact two-layer Lipschitz computation for every p—is unsupported.

The treatment of p<1 has additional gaps. The appendix's XP argument invokes a dual norm even though an L_p quasinorm for p<1 has no dual norm in the stated sense, and the hardness proof explicitly handles only fixed rational p while Theorem 6.2 claims every real p in (0,infinity]. Computational representation issues for arbitrary real p are not addressed.

Corollary 4.3 reduces to multiplicatively approximating an optimum that is 1 in yes-instances but can be negative in no-instances. Standard multiplicative-approximation guarantees are defined for nonnegative objectives/optima and do not justify distinguishing these cases. The paper needs a precise approximation definition and a construction ensuring a valid nonnegative gap.

The proof of Theorem 7.1 incorrectly transfers an approximation of the centered zonotope Z(A)-c back to the paper's uncentered representation Z(A)=sum_i conv({0,a_i}). From an approximation by the symmetric zonotope Z((B'^T,-B'^T)), defining columns as 2b'_i+c does not implement translation by c and generally changes the center by a factor depending on the number of columns. The displayed containment therefore does not follow, undermining Theorems 7.1 and 7.2 as written.

The paper sometimes describes zonotope containment itself as W[1]-hard, whereas the reduction establishes W[1]-hardness of non-containment; containment receives the corresponding complementary hardness characterization unless an additional class-closure argument is stated. Given multiple serious flaws affecting central claimed results, the otherwise promising verification reduction is insufficient for acceptance in the current form.

strengths: The reduction from Multicolored Clique to two-layer ReLU positivity is conceptually interesting and appears to yield meaningful W[1]-hardness and ETH-based lower bounds with input dimension linear in the clique size.
The paper connects neural-network verification with zonotope non-containment in a potentially useful way, bringing together parameterized complexity, computational geometry, and verification.
The spike and penalty gadgets are intuitive, illustrated clearly, and accompanied by relatively detailed proofs.
The theoretical scope is broad, covering positivity, surjectivity, zero-function testing, Lipschitz computation, input-convex networks, and zonotope norm maximization.
weaknesses: The proof of the central Lipschitz-hardness result (Theorem 6.2) relies on the false claim that every positively homogeneous CPWL function satisfies L_p(f)=max_{||x||_p<=1}|f(x)|. Positive homogeneity only immediately gives the latter quantity as a lower bound on the global Lipschitz constant. For a nonconvex CPWL function, a linear region can have a large gradient even when the corresponding maximizing gradient direction does not lie in that region. A difference of two ReLUs with nearly parallel normals provides a simple counterexample. Consequently, the inequalities and gap construction on pages 18–20 do not establish Theorem 6.2.

Theorem 7.1 is not supported by its proof. The cited subspace-embedding result approximates the support function of the centered zonotope Z(A)-c. The manuscript then attempts to convert this into an approximation of the uncentered zonotope by defining columns a'_i=2b'_i+c. Adding c to every generator introduces the translation repeatedly and does not produce c plus the centered approximation. Thus the claimed containment for Z(A') does not follow, undermining Theorems 7.1 and 7.2.

Corollary 4.3 uses a gap in which the optimum is 1 in yes-instances and at most 0 in no-instances to claim hardness of approximation within any multiplicative factor. Standard multiplicative approximation guarantees are not well-defined or informative for objectives with nonpositive optimum. No precise approximation definition or transformation to a nonnegative objective is supplied.

The treatment of p<1 is mathematically inconsistent. The paper invokes dual norms where the L_p quantity is only a quasinorm, and the proof for p<1 is explicitly restricted to fixed rational p even though Theorem 6.2 claims every real p in (0,∞]. The computational representation of an arbitrary real p is also unspecified.

The title and several high-level statements concern zonotope containment, but the established parameterized reduction is to non-containment. W[1]-hardness of the complement does not directly establish W[1]-hardness of containment; the distinction between W[1]-hardness and co-W[1]-hardness needs to be stated carefully.

Several statements are overly broad or insufficiently formal, including “any multiplicative factor,” the dependence of running times on network depth, and claims that enumeration algorithms are essentially optimal. There are also repeated indexing errors in edge labels, such as using ω_{l,i} where ω_{l,j} is intended.

Although the positivity/non-containment reduction may constitute a valid core contribution, multiple prominently advertised theorems are invalid as written. These are central abstract-level claims rather than minor gaps, so the manuscript is not technically sound enough for acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/fb934e9d9c874efea7debf4991dfb403/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses important open questions connecting neural-network verification, parameterized complexity, and zonotope containment.

The multicolored-clique reduction using Sidon labels and spike/penalty gadgets is elegant and appears to establish meaningful W[1]-hardness results for 2-layer ReLU positivity. Homogenization then gives useful consequences for surjectivity and zonotope non-containment.

The parameter dependence is carefully tracked: the constructed input dimension is linear in the clique parameter, enabling ETH-based lower bounds that match the exponent of natural region- or vertex-enumeration algorithms.

The paper is generally well organized, clearly motivated, and unusually broad for a theoretical contribution. It provides proof details in the appendix and also discusses tractable special cases and geometric interpretations.
weaknesses: The proof of Theorem 6.2 contains a major technical error. It asserts that every positively homogeneous CPWL function satisfies Lp(f)=max_{||x||p<=1}|f(x)|. This is not generally true for nonconvex positively homogeneous CPWL functions: the Lipschitz constant is controlled by the norms of local gradients, whereas values along rays from the origin need not expose those gradients.

The specific scaling argument in Theorem 6.2 makes the failure especially concrete. Scaling only the homogenizing y-coefficients moves and narrows the spike gadgets and reduces their height on y=1, but it does not reduce their slopes with respect to the original x variables (e.g., the coefficients 8 and 4 remain unchanged). Consequently, the constructed network's Lipschitz constant does not obey the claimed O(epsilon) upper bound. This invalidates the separation used to prove the prominent 2-layer Lipschitz-hardness result.

Theorem 7.1 also appears incorrect as written. Lewis-weight sampling approximates the centered symmetric zonotope Z(A)-c, but the proposed conversion A'=(2b'_1+c,...,2b'_r+c) does not restore the translation c: adding c to every generator changes the center by roughly r c/2. Therefore, the stated uncentered containment relation does not follow, and Theorem 7.2 is unsupported.

Corollary 4.3 uses a multiplicative approximation to distinguish an optimum of 1 from an optimum that may be nonpositive. Multiplicative approximation is normally defined only for nonnegative objectives, and no alternative definition or promise is supplied. The reduction therefore needs reformulation, such as a genuine 0-versus-positive nonnegative gap.

There are additional definitional inconsistencies around p<1 and p=0: dual-norm reasoning is invoked where no norm dual exists, while different statements alternately use p in [0,infinity] and (0,infinity]. Several indexing mistakes in the edge-label notation further hinder verification.

Although the positivity, surjectivity, and zonotope hardness results remain valuable, the flaws affect multiple headline contributions in the abstract. Correcting them appears to require new arguments rather than local edits, so the submission is not technically sound enough for acceptance in its present form.

strengths: The paper makes a broad and potentially significant theoretical contribution, resolving open parameterized-complexity questions for ReLU positivity, surjectivity, injectivity, Lipschitz computation, and zonotope containment.

The reductions connect network depth to successive levels of the W-hierarchy and yield ETH lower bounds that largely match the stated enumeration algorithms; this is a conceptually appealing account of the combined curse of dimension and depth.
The Multicolored Clique construction is explicit and intuitive, using Sidon-set labels and node/edge spike gadgets to obtain a useful constant gap.
The paper includes meaningful positive results for input-convex networks and generally provides detailed constructions, theorem statements, and proofs rather than relying on informal arguments.
The exposition and visual summary are strong for a technically dense paper, and the relationship between ReLU networks, support functions, Newton polytopes, and zonotopes is well motivated.
weaknesses: Theorem 8.1 and its proof contain a serious error. The subspace embedding approximates the centered zonotope Z(A)-c, but the argument then claims an approximation of the uncentered zonotope Z(A). Defining A'=(2b'_1+c,...,2b'_r+c) does not restore the translation: its center is sum_i b'_i+r c/2, not c. Even the one-dimensional exact case exposes the invalid construction. More fundamentally, containment after dilation about the origin does not follow from containment after centering. Consequently, Theorem 8.2 and the claimed randomized FPT approximation are unsupported as written.

The erroneous approximation section is presented as a substantive contribution in the introduction and conclusion. Although it appears separable from the main hardness results, it cannot be repaired by a minor algebraic correction; the authors must either establish a center-preserving sparsification theorem with the required origin-based containment or remove/ substantially weaken these results.

Several proofs rely on terse assertions that important homogenization conditions hold for every input, or that particular gradient bounds propagate through all formula-simulation layers. Given the complexity of the constructions, these claims warrant explicit algebraic verification, especially in Theorems 5.4 and 7.4.

The Lipschitz decision problem assumes an oracle for exact Lp-norm comparison. This makes the computational model and membership results less standard, particularly for arbitrary real p; the paper should clearly restrict how p is represented and distinguish oracle-relative upper bounds from ordinary bit-complexity results.

There are smaller formal imprecisions, such as Lemma 7.2 describing full-dimensional polyhedra as pairwise disjoint while covering all of R^d, where disjoint interiors is presumably intended. The manuscript would benefit from a careful consistency pass over definitions and quantifiers.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/354ef8e78d1d4e55a998f6abb1f8c53d/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses important open questions and gives a broad set of parameterized-complexity results connecting ReLU depth to the W-hierarchy.
The Sidon-set spike construction for reducing Multicolored Clique to shallow-network positivity is creative and potentially useful beyond this paper.

The paper usefully pairs hardness results with enumeration-based upper bounds and ETH lower bounds, providing a relatively unified complexity picture for positivity, surjectivity, Lipschitz computation, injectivity, and zonotope containment.
The presentation includes a helpful summary table, illustrative gadget figures, and substantial proof detail. The main reductions appear largely self-contained.
The zonotope interpretation and discussion of input-convex networks broaden the relevance beyond neural-network verification.
weaknesses: Theorem 8.1 contains a concrete algebraic error. After sparsifying the centered zonotope, the proof sets A'=(2b'_1+c,...,2b'_r+c), but adding c to every generator does not translate the zonotope by c. For example, with d=n=r=1, A=(2), c=1, and the exact embedding B'=B=(1), the construction gives A'=(3), so Z(A')=[0,3] rather than Z(A)=[0,2]. Thus the claimed containment does not follow, invalidating the proof of Theorem 8.1 and consequently Theorem 8.2 and the advertised randomized approximation contribution.

The multiplicative-approximation claims are not formally defined. In Corollary 5.5 the reduction distinguishes an optimum greater than zero from one at most zero, but conventional multiplicative approximation requires a nonnegative objective and a precisely specified guarantee. The paper neither proves that the no-case optimum is exactly zero nor states how approximation is defined for a negative optimum.

Several consequential steps are asserted too tersely. In the deeper homogenized reductions, the conditions W2(W1x+b1)=0 and h(x,0)=0 are repeatedly said to hold by cancellation without explicit layer-by-layer verification. These identities are essential to excluding spurious positive points after homogenization.

The surjectivity reduction states that the constructed homogeneous network satisfies f(0,1)<0, but this is not established for all formula shapes; for example, the even-depth construction can give zero when the outermost conjunction has a single child unless an unstated preprocessing step is applied.

The treatment of arbitrary p in (0,infinity] relies on an unspecified norm-comparison oracle. The computational model, whether p is fixed or encoded, and the representation of thresholds should be stated more carefully for the exact-computation claims.

The paper overstates that it has settled the landscape 'almost completely' despite leaving completeness and even finite-level W-membership open, and despite substantial overlap with concurrent 2026 hardness results for zonotope norm maximization.

Although the central hardness program is promising, a demonstrably false theorem supporting a claimed contribution, combined with underspecified approximation statements and gaps in some reduction details, is a meaningful soundness issue rather than a minor presentational defect.

strengths: The paper makes a broad, technically meaningful contribution by relating bounded-depth ReLU networks to successive levels of the W-hierarchy. The W[ℓ−1]-hardness results for positivity and surjectivity, together with the depth-dependent results for Lipschitz constants and injectivity, substantially clarify the parameterized complexity landscape.
The W[1]-hardness of zonotope non-containment with respect to ambient dimension resolves a concrete open problem and is independently relevant to computational geometry, control, and verification.

The reductions are generally explicit and constructive. The Sidon-set clique construction, homogenization argument, Boolean-formula simulation, and ETH-based lower bounds form a coherent technical framework rather than a collection of unrelated results.

The paper complements hardness results with enumeration upper bounds and tractable cases for input-convex networks. Its organization, overview table, figures, and discussion of prior and concurrent work make an unusually large set of results reasonably accessible.
weaknesses: The proof of Theorem 8.1 contains a serious error. From an approximation of the centered zonotope Z(A)−c by Z((B′ᵀ,−B′ᵀ)), the paper sets the columns of A′ to 2b′ᵢ+c and claims the corresponding uncentered zonotopes approximate one another. This does not follow: adding c to every generator is not the same as translating the zonotope by c, and it changes the center by an amount depending on the number of generators. Even in the one-dimensional exact case A=[1], c=1/2, and B′=[1/2], the stated construction gives A′=[3/2], not Z(A). Consequently, Theorems 8.1 and 8.2 are not established as written. This section needs a corrected representation that explicitly retains the center, or removal of the claimed result.

Several statements would benefit from more precise computational formulations. In particular, the input representation or oracle model for arbitrary real p is only briefly stipulated, while some claims quantify over every p∈(0,∞]; the exact domain and convention for multiplicative approximation of network maxima should also be stated consistently in each result.

The scope is very large, and some secondary corollaries receive only terse arguments. More explicit layer-count bookkeeping and formal verification of the homogenization conditions in the deeper constructions would make the central proofs easier to audit.

Recent concurrent results already establish parts of the Lipschitz and zonotope norm-maximization landscape, reducing the novelty of those particular components. The main verification and zonotope-containment hardness results nevertheless remain significant.
